class.name: PhysXFlow3D
class.brief_description: NVIDIA Flow smoke, fire and dust, provided by the PhysX module.
class.description: Simulates gas with NVIDIA Flow: a sparse, unbounded grid (it grows wherever the gas goes) with pressure projection, vorticity confinement and combustion. It's fed by the [PhysXFlowEmitter3D] nodes whose [member PhysXFlowEmitter3D.flow] points at it (or, with none set, by every emitter when this is the scene's only [PhysXFlow3D]); physics bodies within [member collision_range] of those emitters are solids the gas flows around, and moving bodies push it. Flow runs on Godot's own [RenderingDevice] (Vulkan or Direct3D 12), and [PhysXFlowRenderEffect] draws it into the frame with Flow's own ray marcher, self-shadowed by the scene's first visible [DirectionalLight3D] -- straight from the GPU, at the simulation's full resolution. Nothing is read back to the CPU unless [member cpu_readback] is on. The render effect is installed by itself, without touching anything you save: with no [Compositor] in the world one is created on the [World3D] while flows exist, and a [Compositor] of your own (on a [WorldEnvironment] or [Camera3D]) gets the effect added at the rendering-server level only -- its effects array is never modified. All of it is undone when the world's last flow leaves. [b]Requirements:[/b] an engine built with [code]flow_sdk=[/code], [code]nvflow.dll[/code] and [code]nvflowext.dll[/code] next to the executable (they are loaded at run time -- without them this node shows a warning and stays inert), and the Forward+ or Mobile renderer (not Compatibility, not headless). Flow's shaders are compiled the first time each is used (a fraction of a second on a first run) and kept in Godot's shader cache folder. [b]Units:[/b] meters and m/s, like the rest of the scene; Flow's own tuned defaults are converted at the boundary.

method.name: add_transient_solid
method.description: Adds a sphere solid moving at [param velocity] (m/s) for the next simulation step only: the gas cannot enter it and takes on its velocity there. [PhysXCloth3D] calls it for some of its moving particles when its [member PhysXCloth3D.flow] is set, so a flapping flag stirs and parts the smoke.

method.name: get_stats
method.description: Diagnostics: [code]running[/code], [code]error[/code], [code]start_ms[/code] (grid creation), [code]step_ms[/code], [code]render_calls[/code], [code]render_outputs[/code], [code]readback_bytes[/code], [code]bounds[/code] (the gas, with [member cpu_readback]), [code]active_blocks[/code] (sparse blocks in use, of [member max_blocks]), [code]scatter_lights[/code] / [code]scatter_passes[/code] / [code]scatter_no_source[/code] (see [member light_scattering]: lights picked last step, scattering passes run, frames Flow had no volume to hand over), and Flow's pipeline / pass / resource counts.

method.name: is_running
method.description: Whether Flow is running for this node (see the configuration warnings if not).

method.name: request_velocity
method.description: Keeps the gas velocity read back to the CPU for the next second, for [method sample_velocity]. Call it every step while sampling.

method.name: sample_smoke
method.description: The smoke at [param position] (world space), from the last CPU readback. Needs [member cpu_readback]; returns [code]-1.0[/code] without it. The readback lags a few frames behind the simulation.

method.name: sample_temperature
method.description: The temperature at [param position] (world space), from the last CPU readback, in the same units as [member PhysXFlowEmitter3D.temperature], [member ignition_temperature] and [member temperature_range] -- e.g. how much a fire hurts or how hot a sensor reads. Needs [member cpu_readback]; returns [code]-1.0[/code] without it. The readback lags a few frames behind the simulation.

method.name: sample_velocity
method.description: The gas velocity at [param position] (world space) in metres a second, from the last readback, a few frames behind the simulation. It is read back while [member cpu_readback] is on, while [member push_bodies] has dynamic bodies near the gas, or for a second after [method request_velocity]. Zero outside the gas or without a readback.

members.member: When enabled, the environment's ambient light lights the gas in raster, as it does Godot's volumetric fog: [member Environment.ambient_light_color] mixed with the sky's radiance by [member Environment.ambient_light_sky_contribution], scaled by [member Environment.ambient_light_energy]. Each point is dimmed by all the gas above it, read from a volumetric shadow map built looking straight down (with [member scattering_shadow_steps] at [code]0[/code], not at all), so the inside of a dense plume is darker than its edge. It replaces the flat grey floor Flow's own renderer gives the unlit side of the smoke. It shares the light scattering pass, at [member scattering_resolution]. The path tracer lights the gas with the sky and ambient on its own, so this only affects raster.
The drag coefficient for [member push_bodies]: about [code]1.0[/code] for boxy debris, [code]0.5[/code] for a ball, up to [code]2.0[/code] for flat sheets.
Upward acceleration per unit of temperature: hot gas rises, cool gas hangs. "Up" is opposite the project's default gravity.

When enabled, the gas shadows the scene in raster from the first shadow-casting [DirectionalLight3D]: a volumetric shadow map over the grid, seen from the light, holds the gas's optical depth from the light's side through 32 depth slices, and opaque surfaces in and behind the gas are darkened by the gas between them and the light. It is built once a frame and read by the next frame's opaque pass, and only the Forward+ renderer reads it. The path tracer shadows through the gas on its own, so this only affects raster.
Simulation cell size in meters. Smaller is finer detail and more GPU cost.
Physics bodies near the gas become solids for it. Box, sphere, capsule and cylinder shapes are supported; convex, concave and heightmap shapes are not yet.
The physics layers whose bodies the gas collides with.
How far from this flow's emitters (in meters) bodies are looked for. With [member cpu_readback] on, the area the gas has spread to is searched as well.
Fuel burns when hotter than [member ignition_temperature], releasing heat and smoke.
How fast the gas cools (exponential, per second).

Copy temperature and smoke back to the CPU every few steps, for [method sample_smoke], [method sample_temperature] and the [code]bounds[/code] in [method get_stats]. Off by default: it costs a full field copy each time and isn't needed for rendering.
With [member embers], how many embers the fire throws up a second.

When enabled, a burning fire (emitters feeding fuel with [member combustion] on, or gas hotter than [member ignition_temperature]) throws up glowing embers: small emissive sparks carried up by the plume that drift, cool from yellow-orange to dull red along the blackbody colours of their temperature, and fall. They draw in raster and under the path tracer.

How bright the [member heat_ramp] glow is. [code]0[/code] turns glowing off. The gas glows where it has smoke, as much as it absorbs (in raster through its opacity, in the path tracer through its extinction), so clear hot air does not glow.

When enabled, a burning fire (see [member embers]) lights the scene in raster through a shadowed point light in its flames, coloured by [member heat_ramp] and pulsing at the frequency real flames puff at for the fire's width, [code]1.5 / sqrt(width)[/code] times a second (Cetegen and Ahmed 1993), about twice a second for a campfire. The gas's own glow lights nothing in raster, so without it a fire leaves the ground around it dark. The path tracer uses it too, as the flame's light source: the gas's glow would light the ground only when a bounce ray happens to hit it, so its glow then shows only to camera and mirror rays and the fire is not counted twice.

Scales the [member fire_light]. It already grows with the burning area. The light scatters in the gas at a tenth of its strength ([member Light3D.light_volumetric_fog_energy]), so it does not wash the flames it stands in into an orange haze.

When enabled, gas never goes below [member floor_height]: a wide solid lies under it (it reserves no blocks and holds no gas). Colliders can't describe terrain heightmaps or trimeshes, so without a floor gas sinks into the ground and spends the grid's blocks there.
The world height of the floor's top (used when [member floor_enabled] is on).

How the gas glows by temperature, from [code]0[/code] to [member temperature_range]: each color is the glow at that temperature, its alpha how much it glows instead of showing the lit smoke. Empty uses a blackbody: [code]0[/code] to [member temperature_range] spans 600 K to 1,500 K, coloured as a blackbody at that temperature and as bright as Planck's law makes it at 580 nm (alpha above [code]1[/code] at the top), so a flame has a bright core and sharp tongues and the cooler gas over it reads as smoke.
The temperature above which fuel burns (see [member combustion]).

When enabled, nearby [OmniLight3D] and [SpotLight3D] nodes light the gas: each glows in the smoke in its own color, fading with distance the way it fades on surfaces (its [member OmniLight3D.omni_range] / [member SpotLight3D.spot_range], [member OmniLight3D.omni_attenuation] / [member SpotLight3D.spot_attenuation], spot cone), dimmed by the gas between it and each point and by the gas in front of the camera. Flow's own renderer only lights the gas with the scene's first [DirectionalLight3D]; this is an extra pass over the pixels the gas covers. Turn it off where the gas has no lights near it. Up to [member scattering_max_lights] lights are used, the strongest at the gas first. Each light's [member Light3D.light_volumetric_fog_energy] scales its glow, as it does for Godot's volumetric fog: set it to [code]0[/code] to keep a light out of the gas.

The most sparse blocks the gas may take up -- a GPU memory budget, since Flow reserves memory for all of them when the grid starts (about 0.45 MB a block: the default 1024 is roughly 0.5 GB). A small plume uses a few hundred; [method get_stats] reports [code]active_blocks[/code]. Gas that would need more is cut off, with a warning. Changing it restarts the simulation.

When enabled, the gas pushes the dynamic bodies in it (debris, Blast pieces, crates) with quadratic drag, [code]0.5 * 1.2 * body_drag * A * |u - v| * (u - v)[/code], where [code]u[/code] is the gas velocity, [code]v[/code] the body's and [code]A[/code] the shape's mean projected area (its surface over four). A blast's front or a fire's updraft carries light debris, as NVIDIA APEX Turbulence did. The bodies push back as moving solids through [member collide_with_bodies]. The gas velocity is read back while such bodies are near it, a few frames late.

With [member light_scattering], how much the gas scatters light forward (toward a camera looking at the light) rather than evenly in every direction: [code]0[/code] glows the same from every side, higher values make a bright halo when looking toward a light, negative values light the gas most when the light is behind the camera.
With [member light_scattering], the most lights that glow in the gas at once (the strongest at it). Each one costs a short march toward it for every step of every pixel the gas covers.

With [member light_scattering], which kinds of light have their glow in the gas blocked by scene objects: each point reads the light's own shadow (the one Godot already renders for meshes, so only for lights with [member Light3D.shadow_enabled]), the way Godot's volumetric fog does, so pillars in front of a light cast dark shafts through the gas. One shadow lookup per shadowed light per step; untick a kind to save it. (The [DirectionalLight3D] already shades the gas through the gas itself; its scene shadows aren't read yet.) To light the gas from inside an object (a lamp in a glowing block), keep the object from shadowing its own light: put it on a render layer of its own and leave that layer out of the light's [member Light3D.shadow_caster_mask].

With [member light_scattering], the resolution the glow is worked out at. Scattered light and its shadows in a gas are soft, so [constant SCATTERING_RESOLUTION_QUARTER] (the default) reads the same as full at about a sixth of the cost; the result is scaled up depth-aware, so the glow doesn't bleed onto the edges of objects in front of the gas. [constant SCATTERING_RESOLUTION_HALF] or [constant SCATTERING_RESOLUTION_FULL] sharpen the edges of the shadows in the glow, for close-ups.
With [member light_scattering], how far (in meters) each point looks toward a light for gas that dims it. Beyond that, gas between a point and the light is ignored.

With [member light_scattering], the steps of the march toward each light that lets the gas shade itself (a light inside thick smoke glows near it and dims further in). [code]0[/code] skips it: cheaper, but light then reaches every point as if through clear air.
With [member light_scattering], a multiplier on the light the gas scatters. The glow is colored by [member smoke_color].

When enabled, the light scattering pass ([member light_scattering], [member ambient_scattering], [member sun_scattering]) moves its march's start offset every frame and blends the result with the previous frames, reprojected and clamped to the current frame's neighbourhood, as volumetric fog does. The step pattern then averages out instead of showing as bands at the gas's edges. History is dropped where the scene behind the gas moves, and when the pass runs for more than one view in a frame only the first view is blended.

How far the self-shadowing reaches toward the light, in steps of three quarters of a cell (48 is about 1.8 m at the default [member cell_size]). Too few for the gas's width leaves it lit almost evenly. [code]0[/code] turns self-shadowing off.

The lift per unit of smoke, whatever its temperature (Flow's buoyancy per smoke). Below [code]0[/code] the smoke is heavier than air and sinks, slides down slopes and pools in hollows, like dust, sand or cold fog; above [code]0[/code] it rises on its own. [member buoyancy] still adds the lift from heat.
The smoke's color, lit by the scene's sun: white steam, gray or black smoke, brown dust, colored signal smoke. See also [member smoke_ramp].
Opacity per meter, per unit of smoke. Burning fuel makes a lot of smoke, so fire reads dense at the default; plain smoke or dust emitters may want 2-10.
How fast smoke thins out (per second). Lower values let it climb and linger longer.

The smoke's color by temperature, from [code]0[/code] to [member temperature_range] -- e.g. black soot near a fire turning light gray as it cools. Empty uses [member smoke_color] at every temperature. Alpha is ignored (opacity comes from the smoke itself).

When enabled, the scene's [DirectionalLight3D] nodes light the gas in raster through the light scattering pass instead of Flow's own renderer: each with its color, energy and [member Light3D.light_volumetric_fog_energy], the Henyey-Greenstein phase of [member scattering_anisotropy], the gas between the point and the light (for the first directional light all of it, read from the same volumetric shadow map as [member cast_shadows]; for others over [member scattering_shadow_reach] in [member scattering_shadow_steps] steps; with a multiple-scattering approximation), and the light's shadow cascades, so a wall between the sun and the smoke shades it as it shades Godot's volumetric fog. Flow's renderer then only draws the smoke's opacity and its glow. The path tracer lights the gas on its own, so this only affects raster.
The temperature at the end of [member heat_ramp].

When enabled, the ground under the gas is a solid for it, so smoke and dust lie on slopes, run down them and pool in hollows instead of sinking into the terrain. The ground is laid as tiles of [member terrain_floor_spacing], each tilted to the local slope and overlapping its neighbours, in the region the gas and its emitters cover. The heights come from [member terrain_path], or else from a ray straight down that only counts static bodies on [member collision_mask]; ground made of boxes, spheres or capsules is already a solid through [member collide_with_bodies] and gets no tiles. Heights are re-read once a second. A heightmap has no overhangs, so gas can't go under arches or into caves on the terrain itself.
The width of a [member terrain_floor] tile, in meters. A wide region uses wider tiles (doubling) so it stays within 32 tiles a side.

The terrain the [member terrain_floor] reads heights from: a TerrainDeformer3D, a baked TerrainDataMap3D, a TerrainGenerator3D, Terrain3D, or any node with [code]get_height(position)[/code]. Empty: a ray down onto static bodies.
Vorticity confinement: keeps small swirls alive for rolling, billowing gas.

constants.constant: The glow is worked out for every pixel.
Half the resolution each way (a quarter of the pixels), scaled up depth-aware.
A quarter of the resolution each way, scaled up depth-aware.
[OmniLight3D] shadows block their glow in the gas.
[SpotLight3D] shadows block their glow in the gas.
